title: VPC Traffic Validation and mTLS Hardening — Runbook (RBAC v2 + Audit Schema + SIEM Export)
body:
Purpose:
This runbook describes a reproducible process for validating VPC traffic controls and hardening mutual-TLS (mTLS) in Private Deployments, while producing audit evidence that can be exported to SIEM. It focuses on three integration points: RBAC v2 mapping for network operations, the audit log schema we emit, and an evidence automation pattern for compliance reviews.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Private deployments (VPC or on-prem) using the Redwood Private control plane.
- Assumes service mesh or sidecar proxy (Envoy) is available and mTLS is handled at the data plane.
- Assumes central Audit Forwarder that can push structured events to SIEM (Splunk/Elastic/Datadog).
- This is a validation + evidence runbook, not the initial implementation spec.

Quick reference checklist (run these in order):
1) Inventory: list subnets, route tables, NACLs, firewall rules, and peering links for the environment under test.
2) Baseline tests: ensure expected flow matrix (who should reach who) is codified in a CSV/manifest.
3) mTLS smoke: confirm TLS handshake success rate and certificate identity mapping for service principals.
4) RBAC v2: verify network-role bindings and admin overrides are scoped correctly.
5) Audit injection: run synthetic traffic that triggers audit events and ensure they reach SIEM.
6) Evidence bundle: auto-collect configs, log extracts, and tracer snippets into structured archive for auditors.

Inventory template (CSV columns):
- namespace, service, subnet, cidr, egress_allowed_to, ingress_allowed_from, expected_ports, expected_protocol, owner

Sample traffic matrix entry (plain text):
- analytics.namespace, analytics-worker, subnet-analytics-1, 10.20.40.0/24, none, 10.20.10.0/24, 443/TCP, service-owners@redwood.ai

mTLS validation steps:
- Step A: Confirm control-plane issued leaf certs have SAN entries matching service principal: service://<namespace>/<service-name>. Example CN: service-analytics@redwood.
- Step B: From a test pod, run openssl s_client -connect <peer-ip>:<port> -servername <expected-name> and confirm certificate Subject and OCSP stapling (if enabled).
- Step C: Check proxy logs for TLS handshake error codes (Envoy: TLS handshake_failed and xds logs).
- Step D: Rotate a test cert (short TTL) and validate zero-downtime rotation using the recommended rolling restart sequence.

Firewall rule templates (high-level):
- Principle: deny-by-default with explicit allow rules. Keep egress minimal.
- Example: Allow-only mesh-control-plane -> control-plane-endpoint (TCP 15010, 9901 health)
- Example CIDR rule: allow kube-api -> mgmt-subnet: TCP 6443 from jump-box only
- Cloud snippet (GCP-like pseudo):
  - allow tcp:443 from 10.20.10.0/24 to 10.20.40.0/24 (service mesh ingress)
  - deny tcp:0-1023 from 0.0.0.0/0 to private-subnets

RBAC v2 mapping (network ops lens):
- Roles (short): network-observer, network-operator, network-admin, security-auditor
- Minimal bindings example (YAML-like plain text):
  - network-observer: read-only access to firewall configs and flow logs, no token issuance
  - network-operator: can modify firewall rules in staging and can request production changes via PR + approval
  - network-admin: emergency Override (requires 2FA + ticket)
  - security-auditor: read access to audit logs and evidence bundles only

Mapping guidance: tie each role to a set of permitted actions in the audit schema (see below) so SIEM and compliance tooling can filter by role identity.

Audit log schema (structured JSON example as emitted by the Audit Forwarder — below is sample event text, included here as a string to show fields):
{
  "event_id": "evt-20241115-0001",
  "timestamp": "2024-11-15T14:22:31Z",
  "actor": { "id": "user:daniel.kim@redwood.ai", "roles": ["network-operator"] },
  "action": "firewall.update",
  "target": { "type": "firewall_rule", "id": "fw-prod-analytics-03" },
  "result": "success",
  "details": { "old_rule": "deny all", "new_rule": "allow tcp 443 from 10.20.10.0/24" },
  "evidence_refs": [ "s3://redwood-evidence/prod/fw-change-20241115.tar.gz" ]
}

Required audit fields (explainers):
- event_id: globally unique, prefixed with env and date
- timestamp: ISO8601 UTC
- actor.id: canonical principal (user: or svc: prefix)
- actor.roles: list of active RBAC v2 roles used to authorize action
- action: namespaced action ("firewall.update", "mtls.cert.rotate", "flow-test.synthetic")
- target.type/id: what resource was affected
- result: success|failure|partial
- evidence_refs: array of URIs pointing to the evidence bundle (S3/GCS/HTTP)

SIEM export mapping and recommended parsers:
- Normalize fields to: event_time, user_principal, role_list, action_name, resource_type, resource_id, status, evidence_uri, raw_payload
- Splunk/Elastic ingestion: tag events with env=prod|staging|dev and add ingest_time. Use the event_id as the document id to dedupe.
- Example KQL for Elastic: 
  event.action:firewall.update AND result:failure | top 20 actor.id
- Detection idea: high-frequency rule changes by same user within short window -> auto quarantine of the identity and create a papertrail ticket.

Evidence automation pattern (high-level):
1) Trigger: any production firewall/mTLS/mesh config change triggers a CI job (GH action or Jenkins) that collects: current infra-as-code diff, running proxy configs, flow logs for last 15 minutes, audit-forwarder event(s), and a 60s tcpdump sample (pcap) for the affected subnets.
2) Build: package files into a compressed tar with manifest.json listing files and checksums.
3) Store: push to secure bucket with immutability (S3 object lock or GCS retention) and generate evidence URI (S3 path).
4) Emit: attach evidence URI to the emitted audit event (evidence_refs) and forward to SIEM.
5) Retention: default 365 days for high-severity changes; 90 days for routine changes (configurable per compliance profile).

Validation play (step-by-step example):
- Example goal: prove that pod A in subnet X cannot reach metadata service on 169.254.169.254 and that mTLS denies client without proper SAN.
- Execute: run synthetic traffic job to attempt curl http://169.254.169.254 from pod A; expect TCP RST or connection timeout. Collect flow logs, envoy logs, and packet capture.
- Audit event: synthetic job posts event action=flow-test.synthetic with outcome=failure and evidence_refs pointing to archive.
- SIEM check: search events by evidence_refs and confirm artifact exists and matches checksums.

Operational traps and mitigations:
- Trap: noisy flow logs fill SIEM. Mitigation: sample at source and forward summary events for high-volume flows; keep raw pcaps only in evidence buckets.
- Trap: RBAC role drift (old roles linger). Mitigation: quarterly role review job that compares bindings to desired state and opens auto-PRs for removal.
- Trap: missing evidence_refs. Mitigation: enforce CI gating policy that rejects infra PRs without the evidence automation hook.

ASCII diagram (logical flows):

  [Admin Console] --(api)--> [Control Plane] --xds--> [Sidecars/Envoy] --(mTLS)--> [Service Pods]
                                       |                                         |
                                       |                                         --> [SIEM Forwarder] -> [SIEM]
                                       |\\
                                       | -- audit-forward -> [Evidence Bucket (S3/GCS)]

Checklist for compliance submission (final artifact):
- inventory.csv (as described above)
- audit_events.jsonl (all emitted events for the change window)
- evidence bundle tar.gz with manifest and checksums
- RBAC-binding-diff (pre/post change)
- firewall-rule-diff and applied rule snapshot
- pcap snippets and proxy logs (redacted if necessary)
- sign-off notes from network-operator and security-auditor

Notes / open questions (for follow-up):
- Decide default retention by compliance tier (proposal: sensitive=365d, standard=90d).
- Determine whether to hash-evidence on ingest and store hash in SIEM for quick verification.
- Add automated test to verify evidence URI resolvability in CI.

Related tickets and follow-ups: see linked_artifacts.

Author notes (working doc):
- This is a runbook draft intended to be converted into CI templates and Confluence final guide. Expect multiple iterations after the first audit run.
